deep.reconstruction:
The page holds two complete discrete-logarithm ('index') tables in the Gaussian integers Z[i]. Each has the same layout as the neighbouring folios (moduli -11+4i, 11, 1+10i, 9+4i). The tables serve Gauss's theory of biquadratic residues: for a prime π with norm p, the index of q gives the quartic character, since q^((p-1)/4) ≡ i^(ind q) (mod π).

Table A. Modulus π = -7+8i, D = N(π) = 49+64 = 113 (prime).
- The residue field Z[i]/π is F_113. Since 8i ≡ 7, we get (my step) i ≡ 7·8^(-1) = 7·99 ≡ 15 (mod 113), and 15^2 = 225 ≡ -1.
- So a+bi corresponds to a+15b mod 113.
- The primitive root is g = 1-4i ≡ 54 (confirmed by the index entry '+1-4i | 1').
- Gauss lists g^k only for k = 0..28 = (p-1)/4. The reason is that g^28 ≡ +i, so every unit residue is i^m·g^k with 0 ≤ k < 28 and m = 0..3. In effect he chose g so that g^((p-1)/4) is exactly +i, not -i.
- The residues are written as small representatives a+bi, roughly the absolutely least: 1, 1-4i, 1+6i, 2-4i, 2+2i, 3+2i, 4-2i, -3-3i, 7, 1-5i, 4-3i, 1+3i, -2, 5, -1+3i, 3, 4+3i, 2+3i, -1-4i, -2-i, 1-i, 5+2i, -1-2i, 6+i, 4, 5-i, -5+2i, -6, i.
- Each entry is g^k reduced mod π. I checked all 29 numerically: 54^k mod 113 gives 1, 54, 91, 55, 32, 33, 87, 65, 7, 39, 72, 46, 111, 5, 44, 3, 49, 47, 52, 96, 99, 35, 82, 21, 4, 103, 25, 107, 15. These agree with a+15b for every listed entry.
- 'Indices der Elementar-Grössen': for each 'elementary quantity' Gauss gives ind(q) mod 112. These are i, 1±i, and the primary-normalised Gaussian primes (a ≡ 1 mod 4, b even) of norm ≤ 113 other than π itself, ending with the conjugate -7-8i.
- Each index is obtained as ind = 28m + k, where q ≡ i^m·g^k with k read from the power table. Examples:
  - 1+i ≡ 16 = g^48;
  - 1+2i = -(-1-2i), giving 56+22 = 78;
  - 5+4i ≡ -3-3i, since 5+4i - (-3-3i) = 8+7i = -i·π, giving 7;
  - -7-8i ≡ 1-i, giving 20.

Table B. Modulus π = -3+10i, D = 109.
- Here i ≡ 3·10^(-1) = 33 (mod 109), and 33^2 ≡ -1.
- The primitive root is g = -1-2i ≡ 42. Its square is -3+4i. The sign is fixed by g^3 = 1-i and by ind(1+2i) = 55 = 54+1.
- Powers are listed for k = 0..27 = (109-1)/4, ending with g^27 ≡ i. Numerically 42^k mod 109 gives 1, 42, 20, 77, 73, 14, 43, 62, 97, 41, 87, 57, 105, 50, 29, 19, 35, 53, 46, 79, 48, 54, 88, 99, 16, 18, 102, 33. These match every listed a+bi, including the blotted ones.
- Indices mod 108 are formed the same way, ind = 27m + k. Examples: 5+2i ≡ -5-i = -i·g^21, giving 102; -3-10i ≡ 4+3i = -i·g^2, giving 83.
- The list stops at -3-10i, the conjugate of the modulus. Primes of norm 113 > 109 are omitted.
errors: Table A (mod -7+8i): the index of 9-4i is written as 3 but should be 34. 9-4i ≡ 2+4i = i·(4-2i) = i·g^6, giving 28+6 = 34. Numerically 9-60 ≡ 62 = 54^34 mod 113, whereas 54^3 ≡ 55 ≡ 2-4i. The likely slip is reducing by 7 instead of by 7-8i (9-4i-7 = 2-4i = g^3). Alternatively a trailing digit 4 is lost or faint in the manuscript.

Table B (mod -3+10i): the index of 5+8i is written as 86 but should be 101. 5+8i ≡ -5+5i ≡ -2-5i = -i·(5-2i) = -i·g^20, giving 81+20 = 101. Numerically 5+8·33 ≡ 51 = 42^101 mod 109, while 42^86 ≡ 83 ≡ -3-4i.
All other 57 power entries and 62 index entries on the page check out exactly.

results.what: Table of powers of a primitive root modulo the Gaussian primes -7+8i (norm 113) and -3+10i (norm 109). Each is listed only up to exponent (p-1)/4, with the root normalised so that g^((p-1)/4) ≡ +i. Residues are written as small Gaussian integers.
results.modern_name: Discrete logarithm (index) tables in the residue field Z[i]/(π) ≅ F_p; primitive roots for Gaussian prime moduli
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (theory of Gaussian integers and biquadratic residues, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum 1828/1832). Real-modulus index tables: Gauss (Disquisitiones 1801), Jacobi's Canon Arithmeticus (1839).

results.what: Indices of i, 1±i and all primary Gaussian primes of norm up to the modulus norm, for the two moduli. Primary here means a ≡ 1 mod 4, b even. These give quartic residue characters via [q/π] = i^(ind q).
results.modern_name: Tables of quartic (biquadratic) residue characters / discrete logs of small primes, as numerical material for biquadratic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (biquadratic reciprocity conjectured and checked numerically; proofs by Jacobi, Eisenstein 1844)

deep.surprise_reason: These are routine computational tables continuing a series on adjacent folios. Gauss is well known to have computed extensively with Gaussian-integer residues for his biquadratic-reciprocity work. The only notable detail is the systematic normalisation g^((p-1)/4) ≡ +i, which halves the table to (p-1)/4 rows. The page also contains two index slips.

Table B, last index entry: the blotted element is -3-10i (index 83, verified).
The crossed-out '43of 2' at the top right is an archival/foliation mark, not mathematics; the circled (20) is the folio number.
